paragraphs.heading: One phenomenon, three phases
paragraphs.text: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, is a global climate phenomenon that shows up as swings in sea surface temperature over the tropical Pacific Ocean. It is one phenomenon with three recurring phases: El Niño, La Niña and neutral. El Niño is the warming phase of the sea surface temperature and La Niña is the cooling phase. The Southern Oscillation is the atmospheric oscillation that goes with it, coupled with the change in sea temperature. It is a swing in surface air pressure between the tropical eastern Pacific and the tropical western Pacific.

paragraphs.heading: The Pacific in its usual state
paragraphs.text: On average, the surface of the tropical East Pacific is cooler than that of the tropical West Pacific by roughly 8–10 °C (14–18 °F). Near the equator, strong trade winds push water out of the East Pacific and into the West Pacific, and the Sun slowly warms this water as it moves west. One result is that the sea near Indonesia typically stands about 0.5 m (1.5 ft) higher than the sea near Peru. The warm surface water collects in the west, so the thermocline lies much deeper there. The thermocline is the transitional zone between the warmer water near the surface and the cooler water of the deep ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Why the east stays cool
paragraphs.text: In the East Pacific, cooler deep water replaces the surface water that has moved away, rising to the surface in a process called upwelling. The Humboldt Current, which flows north, also carries colder Southern Ocean water into the tropics of the East Pacific. Together, this current and upwelling maintain an area of cooler ocean water off the coast of Peru.

paragraphs.heading: How El Niño builds
paragraphs.text: The Bjerknes feedback, named after Jacob Bjerknes, is a key mechanism of ENSO. In it, changes in the atmosphere alter sea temperatures, and these in turn alter the winds, in a positive feedback. When the easterly trade winds weaken, warm surface water surges east and upwelling on the equator is reduced. That leads to warmer sea surface temperatures, called El Niño, and to even weaker trade winds. Ultimately the warm water in the western tropical Pacific is depleted enough that conditions return to normal. Exactly which mechanisms cause the oscillation is unclear, and they are being studied.

paragraphs.heading: Rhythm and weather
paragraphs.text: ENSO switches between El Niño, La Niña and neutral states in an irregular pattern, but the cycle comes round roughly every two to seven years, with varying intensity. The phenomenon tends to be strongest in the northern hemisphere winter, although impacts in particular regions may peak at different times. ENSO is not easily predicted, but many weather organisations monitor it carefully. The climate across much of the tropics and subtropics is affected. El Niño and La Niña disrupt normal weather patterns, which can bring intense storms to some places and droughts to others.

paragraphs.heading: Global temperature and people
paragraphs.text: El Niño events cause short-term spikes, about a year long, in global average surface temperature, and La Niña events cause short-term surface cooling. As a result, how often El Niño occurs compared with La Niña can shape the trend in global temperature over timescales of around ten years. Developing countries that border the Pacific Ocean and depend on agriculture and fishing are the ones ENSO affects most. Future trends in ENSO under climate change are uncertain, although climate change worsens the effects of the droughts and floods associated with it.

paragraphs.heading: Where the names come from
paragraphs.text: El Niño is Spanish for "The Boy". An early recorded use of the term in a climate context came in 1892, when Captain Camilo Carrillo told the geographical society congress in Lima that Peruvian sailors had a name for a warm current flowing south. They had named it after the Christ Child, since it typically showed up around Christmas. The original phrase was El Niño de Navidad, 'The Christmas Boy'. La Niña, Spanish for "The Girl", is the colder counterpart of El Niño.
